per_question.question: What are the general eligibility criteria for CAP/DA services under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under NC Medicaid, the general eligibility standard for CAP/DA is that the person must meet Medicaid coverage criteria for the service and also meet CAP/DA-specific waiver criteria. In short, the beneficiary must need a nursing-facility level of care, have a documented need for CAP/DA waiver services, be able to remain safely in a private residence or other approved setting with supports, and have an approved service plan. The current authoritative policy is **Clinical Coverage Policy 3K-2, effective Sept. 1, 2025**. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## General criteria

CAP/DA services must meet NC Medicaid’s general coverage standards. The service must be:

- individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis;
- not more than the beneficiary needs;
- safely furnishable;
- not replace an equally effective, more conservative, or less costly statewide alternative; and
- not primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caregiver, or provider.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA), § 3.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## CAP/DA-specific eligibility criteria

Medicaid covers CAP/DA when the beneficiary meets the following specific criteria:

- **Nursing facility level of care:** The person must meet the required HCBS nursing facility level of care as determined by NC Medicaid and need long-term care support at a level typically provided in an institution, tied to a documented medical diagnosis and functional care need, assessed quarterly.
- **Reasonable indication of need:** The completed CAP assessment must show a reasonable indication that the person will need at least one CAP/DA HCBS service within 30 calendar days of evaluation.
- **Approved service plan:** The person must have a signed service plan authorizing one or more waiver services to be provided monthly to help prevent institutionalization through coordinated case management.
- **Short-term equipment/modification/technology option:** Alternatively, a signed service plan may authorize installation of equipment, modification, or technology on a short-term basis to allow the person to return to or remain in a primary private residence and avoid institutional placement; the installation must be completed within three calendar months of service plan approval.
- **Safe community living with supports:** The person must be able to maintain health, safety, and well-being in a primary private residence or other approved location with formal and informal supports.
- **Cost cap:** Paid care needs must be maintainable within the average institutional cost of the CAP/DA waiver.
- **Physician oversight:** The person must have a primary physician who can link and coordinate all medical services.
- **Emergency back-up/disaster plan:** The person must have an emergency back-up and disaster plan identifying who will provide care if key staff are unavailable, if the primary caregiver has an emergency, or during a public health emergency.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA), § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

## Limits / when services are not covered

CAP/DA is not covered if the beneficiary does not meet the eligibility requirements in Section 2.0 or the criteria in Section 3.0, if the service duplicates another provider’s service, or if it is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial.  
[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA), § 4.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)

per_question.question: What DME items are specifically NOT covered by NC Medicaid under the Orthotics and Prosthetics policy, and what general criteria must be met for coverage?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid’s Orthotics & Prosthetics policy does **not** cover certain devices or supplies, and coverage generally requires that the item be medically necessary, ordered by an authorized clinician, and not primarily for convenience.

## Items specifically not covered

Under Clinical Coverage Policy **5B, Orthotics & Prosthetics**, Medicaid does **not** cover:

- **Devices for the beneficiary’s comfort or convenience**
- **Devices for the convenience of the beneficiary’s caregiver(s)**
- **Backup or duplicate devices** kept on hand or at different locations
- **Devices and supplies for residents of nursing facilities**
- **Devices or supplies covered by another agency**
- **Equipment or supplies for beneficiaries receiving hospice care**, as defined in the policy’s coordinating-care section  
  [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 4.2]

## General criteria that must be met for coverage

### Baseline coverage rule
A covered orthotic or prosthetic item must be:

- **Individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis**
- **Not in excess of the beneficiary’s needs**
- Able to be **safely furnished**
- Not replaceable by an **equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide**
- Furnished in a manner **not primarily intended for the convenience** of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider  
  [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.1]

### Additional specific coverage criteria
Orthotics and prosthetics are covered when:

- They are **ordered by a physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner**
- They are **medically necessary to maintain or improve** the beneficiary’s medical, physical, or functional level
- They are **appropriate for use in a noninstitutional setting** where normal life activities take place
- There has been a **documented face-to-face encounter** with the ordering clinician related to the primary reason for the device **within 6 months before initiation**
- The beneficiary’s need for the device is **reviewed at least annually** by the ordering clinician  
  [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1]

### What counts as medically necessary under this policy
The policy further says:

- **Orthotic devices** are medically necessary when needed to **correct or prevent skeletal deformities**, **support or align movable body parts**, or **preserve or improve physical function**
- **Prosthetic devices** are medically necessary when they **replace all or part of the function of a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part**, and the beneficiary needs the prosthesis for **mobility, daily care, or rehabilitation**
- Orthotic and prosthetic devices must also be:
  - a **reasonable and medically necessary** part of the treatment plan,
  - **consistent with the diagnosis and medical condition**, especially functional limitations and symptoms, and
  - of **high quality**, with replacement parts available  
  [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 3.2.1]

## Eligibility point
The policy also requires that the beneficiary be **enrolled in NC Medicaid and eligible for the item or service**, subject to all program requirements in the Medicaid eligibility policy. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), § 2.0]

## Bottom line
In short, NC Medicaid will cover orthotic and prosthetic items only when they are medically necessary, properly ordered, clinically appropriate, and not duplicative or for convenience. It will **not** cover convenience items, backup duplicates, items for nursing-facility residents, items covered elsewhere, or certain equipment/supplies for hospice beneficiaries. [[Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment), §§ 3.1, 3.2.1, 4.2]

I checked amendments for Policy 5B and found no listed amendment notices in the corpus; the authoritative document returned was the current **Orthotics & Prosthetics** policy.

per_question.question: What are the entrance, continued service, and discharge criteria for outpatient behavioral health services in NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid does **not appear to use one single universal set of entrance, continued-service, and discharge criteria for all outpatient behavioral health services**. Instead, those criteria are **service-specific** within the behavioral health clinical coverage policies. The current umbrella policy is [Clinical Coverage Policy 8A, Enhanced Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8a-enhanced-mental-health-and-substance-abuse-services/download?attachment), effective **Jan. 2, 2026**; I also checked amendments and found **no separate amendment notice changing 8A** in the corpus for this answer.

## Governing rule
For outpatient behavioral health services under Policy 8A, admission/continued-stay/discharge criteria depend on the **particular service** being requested or delivered, not just on a general outpatient label. The 8A policy contains separate criteria for services such as Intensive In-Home, Day Treatment, and Psychosocial Rehabilitation. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8A, Enhanced Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8a-enhanced-mental-health-and-substance-abuse-services/download?attachment)

## What I could verify from the policy

### 1. Psychosocial Rehabilitation
#### Entrance / eligibility criteria
A beneficiary qualifies when:
- there is a **mental health diagnosis**;
- the beneficiary has **impaired role functioning** adversely affecting at least two of:
  - employment,
  - management of financial affairs,
  - ability to procure needed public support services,
  - appropriateness of social behavior, or
  - activities of daily living; and
- the beneficiary’s functioning indicates a need for psychosocial rehabilitation because of unmet recovery needs and need to regain skills for personal care, meal preparation, housing, or access to social, vocational, and recreational opportunities in the community. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8A, Enhanced Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8a-enhanced-mental-health-and-substance-abuse-services/download?attachment)

#### Continued service criteria
Continued services are appropriate when any of the following applies:
- initial rehabilitation goals in the PCP have been achieved and additional goals still require services;
- the beneficiary is making satisfactory progress toward rehabilitation goals;
- the beneficiary is making some progress, but interventions need modification to achieve greater gains;
- the beneficiary is not making progress and the rehabilitation goals must be modified to identify more effective interventions; or
- the beneficiary is regressing and the PCP must be modified to identify more effective interventions. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8A, Enhanced Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8a-enhanced-mental-health-and-substance-abuse-services/download?attachment)

#### Discharge criteria
Discharge is indicated when:
- rehabilitation goals have been achieved and a lower level of care is appropriate;
- the beneficiary is not making progress or is regressing and all realistic treatment options in this modality have been exhausted; or
- the beneficiary requires a more intensive level of care or service. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8A, Enhanced Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8a-enhanced-mental-health-and-substance-abuse-services/download?attachment)

---

### 2. Child and Adolescent Day Treatment
#### Entrance / eligibility criteria
The beneficiary must have:
- a **mental health or substance use disorder diagnosis** under DSM-5, other than a sole diagnosis of intellectual/developmental disability;
- for children with substance use disorder, ASAM **Level 2.1** criteria;
- documentation that less restrictive rehabilitative services in the educational setting were unsuccessful;
- behavior causing significant school disruption or significant social withdrawal;
- symptoms that severely impair functioning in an educational setting; and
- no evidence that alternative interventions would be equally or more effective under North Carolina community practice standards. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8A, Enhanced Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8a-enhanced-mental-health-and-substance-abuse-services/download?attachment)

#### Continued service criteria
I could confirm that Policy 8A contains a “Continued Service Criteria” section for this service, but the retrieved text for that section was blank in the corpus, so I **could not verify the exact continued-service wording** from the full section text.

#### Discharge criteria
Discharge is indicated when:
- the beneficiary has achieved goals and no longer needs Day Treatment;
- functioning has improved toward PCP goals, including a plan to transition to a lower level of care or appropriate educational setting;
- the beneficiary is not making progress or is regressing, despite exhausting reasonable strategies and interventions, indicating need for more intensive services;
- the beneficiary or legally responsible person no longer wants Day Treatment; or
- the beneficiary needs a more appropriate best-practice treatment modality. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8A, Enhanced Mental Health and Substance Abuse Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8a-enhanced-mental-health-and-substance-abuse-services/download?attachment)

---

### 3. Intensive In-Home (IIH)
#### Entrance criteria
I could confirm that Policy 8A contains an “Entrance Process” section for IIH, but the section text retrieved from the corpus was blank, so I **could not verify the exact entrance language** from the full text here.

#### Continued service criteria
Likewise, I could confirm that Policy 8A contains a “Continued Service Criteria” section for IIH, but the retrieved full text was blank, so I **could not verify the exact continued-service wording** from the policy text available through the corpus.

#### Discharge criteria
Discharge is indicated when:

- functioning has improved on PCP goals, including a transition plan to step down to a lower level of care;
- the beneficiary is not making progress or is regressing, and reasonable strategies/interventions have been exhausted, indicating need for more intensive services;

per_question.question: How does the EPSDT special provision affect coverage for outpatient therapy services, and what ordering practitioner requirements apply to beneficiaries under 21?
per_question.agent_answer:
For beneficiaries under 21, the EPSDT special provision can expand coverage for outpatient therapy services beyond ordinary policy limits when the service is medically necessary to correct or ameliorate the child’s condition, but it does **not** waive any prior approval requirement. And the service still must be ordered by an authorized ordering practitioner. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (effective Feb. 1, 2025; checked for amendments and returned as current authoritative document).

## EPSDT effect on outpatient therapy coverage

Under Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, the EPSDT special provision applies to Medicaid beneficiaries under age 21 as an **exception to policy limitations**. The policy ties that provision to 42 U.S.C. § 1396d(r) and also makes clear EPSDT does **not** require coverage of services that are unsafe, ineffective, experimental/investigational, or not medical in nature / not generally recognized as accepted medical practice. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, § 2.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment).

For outpatient therapy specifically, the practical effect is that the adult visit caps in Policy 10A are for beneficiaries **21 and older**: 30 visits per calendar year for the listed therapy categories. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, § 5.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment).  
By contrast, for beneficiaries **under 21**, the policy uses **medical-necessity visit guidelines** rather than the adult cap, with speech-language and audiology therapy tied to severity and to the number of medically necessary visits within an authorization period of no more than six months. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, § 5.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment).

The policy’s EPSDT/prior approval rule is explicit: if a service, product, or procedure requires prior approval, being under 21 **does not eliminate** that prior approval requirement. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, “EPSDT and Prior Approval Requirements”](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment).

## Requirements that still apply for beneficiaries under 21

Children and youth under 21 still must meet the discipline-specific medical-necessity standards in the outpatient therapy policy. For example:

- **Speech-language therapy** has specific documented-finding requirements for dysphagia-related treatment and includes pediatric criteria for beneficiaries from birth through age 20. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, § 3.2.1.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment).
- **Audiology/aural rehabilitation** is covered when the beneficiary shows qualifying hearing loss or impaired auditory processing and has one or more specified deficits to initiate therapy. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, § 3.2.1.4](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment).

So EPSDT can help overcome ordinary policy limits for a beneficiary under 21, but it does not erase medical-necessity criteria or prior approval rules.

## Ordering practitioner requirements

Policy 10A lists the following as authorized **ordering practitioners** for these services:

- Medical Doctor (MD)
- Doctor of Osteopathic Medicine (DO)
- Doctor of Podiatric Medicine (DPM)
- Certified Nurse Midwife (CNM)
- Physician Assistant (PA)
- Nurse Practitioner (NP)

[Clinical Coverage Policy 10A, § 3.1.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment).

Based on the text I retrieved, Policy 10A does **not** state a separate, stricter ordering-practitioner category that applies only because the beneficiary is under 21. The under-21 rule affects coverage and visit limits through EPSDT and pediatric medical-necessity standards, but the ordering practitioners listed in § 3.1.2 are the applicable ordering practitioners I could verify in the policy text.

If you want, I can also pull together this answer into a short advocacy-friendly statement for a PA request or appeal.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover Personal Care Services for beneficiaries who live in an assisted living facility?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes—NC Medicaid does cover Personal Care Services (PCS) for some beneficiaries who live in an assisted living-type setting, but only if they meet the congregate-setting PCS eligibility rules.

## Short answer

Coverage is available in certain licensed congregate facilities, including:
- an **Adult Care Home (ACH)**, and
- a **combination home**,

as well as certain licensed group homes. NC Medicaid’s congregate-setting PCS policy says the beneficiary must reside in one of those licensed settings and meet functional and medical criteria. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## What must be true for coverage

Under the congregate PCS policy, the beneficiary must:
- have a medical, mental, physical, or cognitive condition causing functional limitations;
- have unmet needs with enough qualifying **activities of daily living (ADLs)**—specifically:
  - at least **3 of 5 qualifying ADLs with limited hands-on assistance**, or
  - **2 ADLs** if one requires **extensive assistance**, or
  - **2 ADLs** if one requires **full dependence**;
- live in a qualifying licensed congregate facility;
- have PCS needs directly linked to the documented condition;
- be under the ongoing direct care of a physician; and
- be medically stable and not need continuous nursing-level monitoring or supervision. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

The policy also requires, among other things, that:
- no other third-party payer is responsible for the PCS, and
- no family, household member, or informal caregiver is available, willing, and able to provide the authorized services during those times. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 3.2.1](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## What services are covered

If eligible, Medicaid covers PCS in congregate settings for services such as:
- hands-on assistance with qualifying ADLs;
- related cueing, prompting, guiding, or supervision when part of that hands-on assistance;
- certain home management IADLs tied to the qualifying ADLs;
- assistance with medication, adaptive or assistive devices, durable medical equipment, and certain delegated tasks, when policy requirements are met. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Assessment / approval requirements

A PCS assessment is required. The congregate-setting policy says:
- eligibility and authorized service level must be assessed by an independent assessor using NC Medicaid’s approved assessment process;
- for new admissions, the assessment must be **face to face in the beneficiary’s congregate facility**;
- the assessment must verify a **valid facility license**; and
- a **physician attestation of medical necessity** is required. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 5.4.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

There is also a physician referral requirement under the NC Medicaid-3051 PCS request process. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings, § 5.4.2](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

If by “assisted living facility” you mean a **licensed Adult Care Home or similar qualifying congregate facility**, then **yes, NC Medicaid can cover PCS there**—but not automatically. The person must meet the ADL, medical necessity, physician, facility, and assessment requirements in the congregate PCS policy. [State Plan Personal Care Services (PCS) Provided in Congregate Settings](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/media/14986/download?attachment)

I also checked amendment status for the cited PCS congregate policy and found no listed amendments in the corpus; it is treated there as the current authoritative document.

per_question.question: Does NC Medicaid cover chiropractic services under Clinical Coverage Policy 5B?
per_question.agent_answer:
No. Clinical Coverage Policy 5B does **not** cover chiropractic services as such. Policy 5B governs **orthotics and prosthetics** and covers only devices that meet that policy’s criteria, not chiropractic treatment or chiropractic provider services. [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

### Why
Under Policy 5B, NC Medicaid covers **orthotic and prosthetic devices** when they meet the policy’s coverage criteria. The policy describes covered orthotics as devices medically necessary “to correct or prevent skeletal deformities, to support or align movable body parts, or to preserve or improve physical function,” and covered prosthetics as replacement devices for a permanently inoperative, absent, or malfunctioning body part. It also requires that they be ordered by a **physician, physician assistant, or nurse practitioner** and meet other medical-necessity standards. [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

The policy also says a request must fit the definition of an **orthotic or prosthetic** device and be medically necessary under the policy. [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

### What that means for chiropractic care
I could not find any language in Policy 5B stating that **chiropractic services** are covered under that policy. Based on the text I reviewed, 5B is limited to orthotic/prosthetic devices and related coverage rules, not chiropractic treatment.

### Important nuance
If you are really asking about a **back brace, cervical orthosis, or other device** that a chiropractor wants a beneficiary to use, the question becomes whether the item qualifies as a covered **orthotic device under Policy 5B**. But the service of chiropractic treatment itself is not identified as covered under 5B. [Orthotics & Prosthetics](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/5b-orthotics-prosthetics/download?attachment)

I also checked for amendments, and the knowledge base identifies Policy 5B itself as the current authoritative document.

per_question.question: Can a CAP/DA beneficiary transfer between service providers, and what rules govern transfers of eligible beneficiaries?

Yes. A CAP/DA beneficiary can transfer, and the governing transfer rules are laid out in **Section 3.3, “Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries,”** of the current **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)** policy, effective **September 1, 2025**. I also checked amendments for that policy and the current authoritative document remains 3K-2.

## Main rule

Under **Section 3.3**, the **CME must coordinate the transfer to prevent gaps in service provisions**. Before the transfer, the following steps must be completed:

- determine the anticipated start date of service;
- coordinate a transition plan between provider agencies;
- discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- initiate transfer of the electronic health record in the CAP Business System (e-CAP/DA) to the receiving county;
- arrange a home visit within **5 business days** after the beneficiary moves to the new primary residence, so the receiving entity can assess the environment for health and welfare concerns; and
- coordinate services so they begin on the **first date of the transfer**.  
  Source: **Section 3.3, Transfers of Eligible Beneficiaries**, **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**.

## If the beneficiary is transferring to a different county

Section 3.3 gives more specific rules for a CAP/DA beneficiary transferring to another county:

- the transferring CME designee must coordinate with the receiving CME designee on the agreed transfer date, or **within less than 30 calendar days of the request to transfer**;
- both CMEs must discuss and plan for the beneficiary’s health, safety, and well-being;
- the electronic health record must be transferred to the receiving county;
- the receiving CME must arrange a home visit within **5 business days** after the move to assess the new setting and address health and welfare concerns; and
- services must be coordinated to start on the **first date of transfer into the receiving county**.  
  Source: **Section 3.3**, **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**.

## Beneficiary choice of provider

The policy also supports beneficiary choice. Under **Section 5.4.2**, the CAP/DA person-centered service plan must:

- document the **authorized provider name, amount, frequency, and duration** of each service; and
- ensure the beneficiary’s **right to choose among providers** and among Medicaid-enrolled providers, shown by a signed **Freedom of Choice** form.  
  Source: **Section 5.4.2, CAP/DA Person-Centered Service Plan Requirements**, **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**.

So, while Section 3.3 speaks in terms of transfers coordinated by the CME and provider agencies, Section 5.4.2 confirms that the beneficiary has a protected right to choose among providers.

## Provider-side timing rules that help govern transitions

Two supporting provisions help show how the system is supposed to handle a transfer operationally:

- A CME must be able to collaborate with a network of providers so that a service authorization can be accepted within **3 business days** of submission.  
  Source: **Section 6.4.1**, **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**.
- Medicaid providers furnishing CAP/DA waiver services must **accept, decline, or acknowledge service authorizations within 3 business days** in e-CAP.  
  Source: **Section 6.5**, **[Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment)**.

These provisions do not replace Section 3.3, but they reinforce that transfers must be handled promptly and without service interruption.

## Federal regulation

The prefetched frame also pointed to **[42 CFR Part 413](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-413)**, and I checked amendments for that federal regulation as well; the current authoritative document remains 42 CFR Part 413. But the text retrieved from **42 CFR § 413.64** concerns **payments to providers** on a reasonable-cost basis. It does **not** appear to govern CAP/DA beneficiary transfers between service providers. For the transfer question, the controlling NC Medicaid authority in the retrieved materials is **CAP/DA Policy 3K-2, Section 3.3**, with Section 5.4.2 supporting beneficiary provider choice.

## Bottom line

A CAP/DA beneficiary **can transfer between providers/counties**, but the transfer must be **CME-coordinated** and carried out under **Section 3.3** to avoid gaps in services. The required rules include coordination between agencies, planning for health and safety, transfer of records in e-CAP, a **home visit within 5 business days** after the move, and service start on the **first day of the transfer**. The beneficiary’s **right to choose among providers** is separately recognized in **Section 5.4.2**.

per_question.question: Is there a maximum earned income limit for people on HCWD (Health Coverage for Workers with Disabilities), and what premiums apply?
per_question.agent_answer:
No—NC HCWD does **not** impose a maximum **earned income** limit in the materials I found. The policy says the cap is on **unearned income**, not earned income: people with **unearned income above 150% of the federal poverty level (FPL) are not eligible for HCWD**. It also says HCWD “remove[s] limits on countable income except for the 150% of Federal Poverty Level (FPL) cap on unearned income,” while premiums rise as countable income rises. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 01-14, HCWD Phase III](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn01-14.pdf)

## Premiums that apply

Under MA-2180 as amended, the cost-sharing structure is:

- **At or below 150% FPL:** no premium.  
- **Above 150% FPL:** a **$50 annual enrollment fee** applies.  
- **Above 200% FPL:** a **monthly premium** is due **in addition to** the $50 annual enrollment fee.  
- **Above 450% FPL:** the person pays a **full premium**. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-NO-03-25.docx.pdf)

## Current HCWD monthly premium chart
The MA-2180 premium chart has been **updated by Change Notice No. 03-25, effective January 1, 2025**. The underlying MA-2180 manual is therefore amended on this point. [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-NO-03-25.docx.pdf)

The manual text I retrieved gives these premium levels:

| Countable monthly income | Individual monthly premium | Couple monthly premium |
|---|---:|---:|
| 0–150% FPL | $0 | $0 |
| 151–200% FPL | $0 | $0 |
| 201–250% FPL | $196 | $265 |
| 251–300% FPL | $235 | $318 |
| 301–350% FPL | $274 | $370 |
| 351–400% FPL | $313 | $423 |
| 401–450% FPL | $352 | $476 |
| 451% FPL and above | $875 | $875 |

[MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma-2180-3.pdf)

## If you meant the older 2019 premium amounts
There is also a separate **2019 HCWD Premiums (Effective April 1, 2019)** chart, but that chart has since been superseded by later amendments, including the 2025 FPL update. The 2019 chart showed the same structure but lower income-band dollar thresholds. [MA-2180 HEALTH COVERAGE FOR WORKERS WITH DISABILITIES – 2019 HCWD Premiums](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019-health-coverage-for-workers-with-disabilities.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 04-19, 2019 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) And Health Coverage For Workers With Disabilities](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/ma_cn04-19.pdf); [CHANGE NOTICE FOR MANUAL NO. 03-25, 2025 Federal Poverty Level Changes (FPL) Income Changes](https://policies.ncdhhs.gov/wp-content/uploads/CN-NO-03-25.docx.pdf)

If you want, I can also turn this into a quick eligibility screener using a client’s earned income, unearned income, and household size.

per_question.question: What is the federal statutory authority for NC's CAP/DA waiver, and what does the state need to demonstrate in its waiver application?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC’s CAP/DA waiver is a **home- and community-based services waiver under section 1915(c) of the Social Security Act**, as implemented in **42 CFR Part 441, Subpart G**. The federal regulations require the state, in its waiver request, to show both the required **assurances/supporting documentation** and that the waiver serves people who **would otherwise need institutional level of care**, with waiver costs evaluated against the cost of institutional care. See [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301; [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective 9/1/2025, current).

## Federal authority

The controlling federal waiver authority for CAP/DA is the **1915(c) HCBS waiver framework** in [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441). Section 441.301 states that a waiver request under that subpart must include the assurances in § 441.302 and supporting documentation in § 441.303, and applies to home- and community-based services furnished under that waiver authority. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301.

North Carolina’s CAP/DA clinical policy is the state implementation document for this program and describes CAP/DA as the **Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults**, a waiver program with Medicaid eligibility and participation rules. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective 9/1/2025, current).

## What the state must demonstrate in its waiver application

Under **42 CFR 441.301**, the state’s waiver request must demonstrate at least the following:

- **Required assurances and supporting documentation**  
  The request must contain the assurances required by **§ 441.302** and supporting documentation required by **§ 441.303**. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301(a)(1).

- **Whether the state will deny HCBS when waiver costs exceed institutional costs**  
  The state must explain whether it will refuse HCBS to a beneficiary when it can reasonably expect the cost of waiver services to exceed the cost of an equivalent level of care in a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID, as applicable. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301(a)(3).

- **Institutional level-of-care showing**  
  The waiver must provide that services are furnished only to beneficiaries who the state determines **would, in the absence of waiver services, require** the Medicaid-covered level of care provided in a hospital, nursing facility, or ICF/IID, as applicable. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301(b)(1)(iii).

- **Person-centered written plan of care / service plan**  
  Services must be furnished under a **written person-centered service plan** subject to Medicaid agency approval. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301(b)(1)(i), (c)(1)-(2).

- **Target group and service definitions**  
  The state must describe:
  - who will receive the services,
  - the qualifications of the person(s) developing the plan of care,
  - and each waiver service separately and with a definite definition.  
  [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301(b)(2)-(6).

- **Functional-need/person-centered planning protections**  
  The request must show a compliant person-centered planning process, including individual choice, informed decision-making, conflict-of-interest protections, and plan updates as needed. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441), § 441.301(c)(1).

## Public notice requirement before submission

Before submitting a Medicaid demonstration application or extension to CMS, the state must provide public notice and opportunity for comment under **42 CFR 431.408**. That section requires, among other things:

- at least a **30-day public notice and comment period**,
- a comprehensive description of the proposal,
- the specific waiver/expenditure authorities the state believes are necessary,
- at least **two public hearings**, and
- statewide accessibility measures for public participation.  
[42 CFR Part 431](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-431), § 431.408.

## NC implementation point

NC’s current CAP/DA clinical policy shows the state’s operational criteria for coverage and participation, including that services are covered only when eligibility and policy criteria are met. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment), §§ 3.1, 4.1 (effective 9/1/2025, current).

## Bottom line

For CAP/DA, the federal authority is **section 1915(c)** as implemented through **42 CFR Part 441**. In its waiver application, North Carolina must show that the waiver includes the required federal assurances and documentation, identifies the target group and services, uses person-centered planning, and—most importantly—serves individuals who **would otherwise require institutional care**, while addressing whether waiver costs exceed the cost of that institutional level of care. It also must satisfy the applicable public notice process in **42 CFR 431.408** before submission to CMS.

If you want, I can next pull the **specific assurance categories in 42 CFR 441.302 and 441.303** that NC has to document for a 1915(c) waiver.

per_question.question: What are the requirements for home modifications under CAP/DA, and what documentation must the Multidisciplinary Team provide?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under CAP/DA, home modifications must be tied to an identified need in the beneficiary’s service planning, and the beneficiary must work with the Multidisciplinary Team (MDT) to identify needs for “equipment, modification, technology, training and education and goods and services.” The policy also says equipment/modification/technology must be used to improve or maximize the beneficiary’s mobility, safety, independence, community integration, environmental/community accessibility, or address 24/7 coverage concerns. [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) (effective Sept. 1, 2025, current; beneficiary agreement section “I agree to:”); [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 3.4.5 (effective Sept. 1, 2025, current).

## Home modification requirements under CAP/DA

The policy text supports these baseline requirements:

- **The need must be identified through the CAP/DA planning process and MDT collaboration.**
- **The modification must serve a functional or medical purpose**, such as improving:
  - mobility,
  - safety,
  - independence,
  - integration into the community,
  - environmental/community accessibility, or
  - 24-hours-a-day/7-days-a-week coverage concerns.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 3.4.5.

- **Where modifications may be made** includes:
  - the beneficiary’s **primary private residence** owned by the beneficiary or family,
  - a **rented residence** if the modifications are portable,
  - a rented residence when the owner allows the modification,
  - and, for some modifications, a **primary vehicle** of the beneficiary or of the documented legal guardian/primary caregiver.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) section “EQUIPMENT, MODIFICAITON AND TECHNOLOGY.”

- **Examples of covered home modifications** listed in the policy include:
  - ramps,
  - grab bars, safety rails, and handrails,
  - widening doorways/passages for wheelchair or walker access,
  - emergency egress when medically necessary due to physical limitations of the responsible party,
  - bathroom accessibility modifications,
  - bedroom modifications for hospital beds/wheelchairs,
  - kitchen accessibility modifications,
  - floor coverings for ease of ambulation,
  - non-skid surfaces,
  - door handle and door modifications,
  - lifts used primarily inside the home,
  - certain smart-home devices when the beneficiary lives alone and the need is identified in the assessment and person-centered service plan,
  - certain air filtration systems when the policy’s medical criteria are met,
  - and replacement of fixtures, mirrors, and storage space damaged or removed during an approved modification.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) section “EQUIPMENT, MODIFICAITON AND TECHNOLOGY.”

## Documentation the MDT must provide

For equipment, technology, and home modification requests, the policy requires documentation that includes:

- **A recommendation by the MDT** identifying the beneficiary’s need for the requested home modification;
- **The cost** of the item/modification the beneficiary requires;
- **A statement of need in the service plan**;
- **Evidence of medical need** recommended by the MDT or by a physician, when applicable;
- **Shipping costs itemized** in the proposal request;
- **Any other information required for the specific item requested**;
- **Quotes**, when required for purchase, adaptation, or modification, in the number NC Medicaid requires; and
- **Written recommendations from appropriate professionals** when NC Medicaid or its designee determines special circumstances are present.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 5.9.1.

The policy also specifically lists supporting documentation/records for equipment, supply, adaptation, or modification requests:

- **a comprehensive Multidisciplinary declaration of need assessment** completed by the case manager identifying the equipment, technology, supply, adaptation, or modification needs;
- **a copy of the physician’s order**, when applicable;
- **a recommendation by an appropriate professional** identifying the beneficiary’s need for the requested equipment/supply/adaptation/modification;
- **the estimated life of the equipment** and **how long the beneficiary is expected to benefit** from it; and
- **an invoice from the supplier** showing the date provided and cost, with related charges maintained in the CAP Business system.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) section “Limits, Amount And Frequency.”

For requests involving equipment/modification/technology more generally, the policy also requires:

- **a training plan** for the beneficiary/family on use of the equipment, with completion documented by the case manager and signed by the beneficiary or responsible party.  
  [Community Alternatives Program for Disabled Adults (CAP/DA)](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3k-2-community-alternatives-program-disabled-adults-capda/download?attachment) § 5.9.1.

## Practical summary

In short, CAP/DA home modifications must be:
1. tied to an assessed beneficiary need,
2. included in service planning,
3. aimed at safety/accessibility/independence or similar covered purposes, and
4. supported by MDT and, where applicable, physician/professional documentation.

The MDT/case-management documentation should at minimum show:
- the identified need,
- the medical or functional justification,
- the cost and quote information,
- service-plan inclusion,
- any required physician or professional recommendation,
- and related supporting records such as invoices and expected useful life where applicable.

If you want, I can also turn this into a **checklist for an appeal or prior-approval packet**.

per_question.question: How many days of therapeutic leave from a nursing facility does NC Medicaid allow per year, and what conditions must be met?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid allows **up to 60 days of therapeutic leave per calendar year** from a nursing facility bed. No more than **15 consecutive therapeutic leave days** may be taken **without NC Medicaid approval**.  
Cited source: [Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8 Therapeutic Leave, effective **Aug. 7, 2024**; amendment check returned the cited document as the authoritative current document.

## Conditions that must be met

Therapeutic leave must meet all of these conditions:

- It must be **for therapeutic purposes only**.
- It must be **ordered by the resident’s attending physician**.
- Its **necessity must be documented in the resident’s plan of care**.
- The **therapeutic justification for each instance** must be entered into the **resident’s health record**.
- The facility must **reserve the resident’s bed** during the leave.
- The facility may receive **only the reimbursement for that reserved bed** during the absence.
- The facility is paid its **full current Medicaid bed rate** for the reserved bed, but **not for days over the legal limit**.
- The facility must keep a **cumulative record** of therapeutic leave days for audit/reference purposes.
- The resident must be listed as on therapeutic leave on the facility’s **midnight census**.
- Medicaid is billed for approved therapeutic leave days as **regular residence days**.

## Important exclusions

Therapeutic leave does **not** apply when the absence is for the purpose of receiving:

- **inpatient services**, or
- **nursing services provided elsewhere**, or
- services at a **different level of care in the current facility**

**when those services are paid for by Medicaid**.

Also, **ambulance transportation** to the therapeutic leave site is **not reimbursed** by Medicaid for this purpose.  
Source: [Nursing Facilities](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/2b-1-nursing-facilities/download?attachment), § 5.8.

If you want, I can also pull the related NC Medicaid rules on **bed-hold days for hospitalization or other absences**, which are different from therapeutic leave.

per_question.question: If a Private Duty Nursing provider terminates services for a Medicaid beneficiary, what notification requirements must they follow?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. Under NC Medicaid’s PDN policy, if the **Private Duty Nursing (PDN) provider discharges/terminates services**, the provider must notify NC Medicaid as follows:

- **Provider discharge of the beneficiary:**  
  The PDN provider must submit the **DMA-3513 (PDN Discharge Summary Form)** to NC Medicaid **within 5 business days**.  
  Citation: 3G-1, § 5.2.4.1, [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

- **Discharge because another payer/source of nursing coverage will take over:**  
  The provider must **notify NC Medicaid** and submit the **DMA-3513 within 5 business days**. The notice must include:
  - the **last date PDN services were provided and billable to Medicaid**, and
  - the **name of the other source of coverage**.  
  Citation: 3G-1, § 5.2.4.1, [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

- **If the attending physician, rather than the provider, terminates PDN:**  
  The PDN provider must send NC Medicaid, **within 5 business days**:
  - the **attending physician’s order to terminate PDN services**, and
  - the **DMA-3513**.  
  Citation: 3G-1, § 5.2.4.1, [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

Two related points from the same section:

- If services stop because the beneficiary **loses Medicaid eligibility**, or if **no PDN services are provided for 30 consecutive days** for any reason (including hospitalization), the **prior approval process must be started again**.  
  Citation: 3G-1, § 5.2.4.1, [3G-1 Private Duty Nursing for Beneficiaries Age 21 and Older](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3g-1-private-duty-nursing-beneficiaries-age-21-and-older/download?attachment)

per_question.question: What does federal law define as 'home health services' under Medicaid, and where must they be provided?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid law, **“home health services”** are the services listed in **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)** when they are provided to a beneficiary:

- **at the beneficiary’s place of residence**;
- **pursuant to written orders** from a physician, nurse practitioner, clinical nurse specialist, or physician assistant acting under state law for most listed home health services; and
- **as part of a written plan of care** that the ordering practitioner reviews **every 60 days** for nursing, home health aide, and therapy services. For medical supplies, equipment, and appliances, the rule uses the practitioner-order/plan-of-care framework stated in § 440.70(a)(3), with review timing tied to § 440.70(b)(3). [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## What counts as “home health services”
Under **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(b)**, home health services include:

- **Nursing services** provided on a part-time or intermittent basis;
- **Home health aide services**;
- **Medical supplies, equipment, and appliances** suitable for use in settings where normal life activities take place; and
- **Physical therapy, occupational therapy, or speech pathology and audiology services**.  
  [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

The regulation also expressly says that **coverage of home health services cannot be contingent on the beneficiary needing nursing or therapy services**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Where they must be provided
Federal law requires that Medicaid home health services be provided at the beneficiary’s **“place of residence.”** But the regulation also clarifies that this is **not limited to a private house or apartment**.

Under **42 C.F.R. § 440.70(c)(1)**, home health services may be provided in **“any setting in which normal life activities take place,”** except certain excluded settings. The rule also states that **home health services cannot be limited to beneficiaries who are homebound**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Excluded settings
A beneficiary’s “place of residence” for this purpose **does not include**:

- a **hospital**;
- a **nursing facility**; or
- an **intermediate care facility for individuals with intellectual disabilities (ICF/IID)**,

**except** that some home health services may be provided in an ICF/IID if those services are **not required to be provided by the facility** under the applicable federal rules. The regulation also excludes **any setting in which Medicaid payment is or could be made for inpatient services that include room and board**. [42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)

## Short answer
So, federally, Medicaid “home health services” are a defined package of nursing, aide, medical-supply/equipment, and certain therapy services, ordered by an appropriate practitioner and furnished under a written plan of care. They must be provided at the beneficiary’s **place of residence**, meaning generally **any setting where normal life activities occur**, but **not** in a hospital, nursing facility, or most inpatient/room-and-board settings.  
Current authority: **42 C.F.R. § 440.70**, in **[42 CFR Part 440](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-440)**.

per_question.question: How does NC Medicaid define 'terminally ill' for purposes of hospice eligibility, and what certification is required?
per_question.agent_answer:
For NC Medicaid hospice, a person is treated as **“terminally ill” when the certification/recertification supports a life expectancy of six months or less**. The hospice policy’s certification requirements repeatedly tie terminal-illness eligibility to a physician’s clinical judgment and narrative supporting that prognosis, including for later benefit periods where the narrative must explain why the face-to-face clinical findings support **“a life expectancy of six months or less.”** [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment) (effective Mar. 15, 2024), **D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness**.

## Required certification

NC Medicaid requires **written certification of terminal illness for each hospice benefit period**. The hospice provider must obtain the written certification **before submitting a claim for payment**. If the written certification cannot be obtained within two calendar days after the period begins, an **oral certification** must be obtained within those two days, and the written certification must still be obtained before billing. Certifications may be completed **no more than 15 calendar days before** the effective date of election, and recertifications **no more than 15 calendar days before** the next benefit period begins. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), **§ 5.4.1**.

## Who must sign it

For the **initial 90-day benefit period**, the hospice must obtain a written certification from:

- **the hospice medical director or physician member of the interdisciplinary group (IDG)**; and
- **the individual’s attending physician, if the individual has one**.

For **subsequent benefit periods**, only the **hospice medical director or physician member of the IDG** must certify. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), **§ 5.4.3**.

## What the certification must contain

The certification or recertification must include:

- a **physician narrative** briefly synthesizing the clinical information supporting the terminal diagnosis;
- the physician’s attestation that the narrative was composed after reviewing the clinical information and, where applicable, examining the beneficiary;
- a narrative reflecting the beneficiary’s **individual clinical circumstances**;
- the **election period dates** to which the certification applies; and
- the physician’s **signature and date**.

For the **third and later election periods**, the narrative must also explain why the clinical findings from the required face-to-face encounter support a **life expectancy of six months or less**. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), **D. Certification and Recertification of Terminal Illness**.

## Face-to-face recertification requirement

Beginning before the **third benefit period recertification**, and for every recertification after that, a **hospice physician or hospice nurse practitioner** must have a face-to-face encounter with the beneficiary **no more than 30 calendar days before** the recertification, to gather clinical findings supporting continued hospice eligibility. [Hospice Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/3d-hospice-services/download?attachment), **§ 5.4.1**.

I checked amendments for Policy **3D, Hospice Services**, and the corpus shows the cited document as the **current authoritative version** with **no listed amendments**.

per_question.question: What ambulance services are NOT covered by NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid does **not** cover ambulance services outside the policy’s covered-service criteria, and the policy lists several specific non-covered situations and charges.

## Not covered ambulance services

Under NC Medicaid’s Ambulance Services policy, the following are **not covered**:

- **Loaded mileage to a facility that is not the nearest appropriate facility**  
  Medicaid reimburses transport only to the **nearest appropriate facility**. If the destination does not meet that standard, the loaded mileage is not reimbursed. A physician’s staff privileges and the beneficiary’s personal preference do not determine whether a facility is “appropriate.” ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1, effective 12/15/2023)

- **An ambulance is called and no treatment is needed** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

- **False alarm responses** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

- **Situations where the beneficiary refuses all medical services** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

- **Ambulance transport for a medical service that is not itself a Medicaid-covered service** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

- **Commercial airline tickets** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

- **Airstrip fees** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

- **Taxes or separate tax charges**  
  This includes local, state, federal, and similar taxes. ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

- **Separate additional charges for nursing personnel who are employees of a facility or ambulance service** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

- **Waiting fees** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

- **Separate charges for oxygen and other items/supplies provided in transport**  
  Those costs are included in the base rate and are **not separately reimbursable**. ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

- **Any ambulance services other than those listed as covered in § 3.2** ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.2.1.4, effective 12/15/2023)

## General non-coverage limits

Even before the ambulance-specific exclusions, Medicaid also does **not** cover the service if:

- the beneficiary does not meet eligibility requirements in Section 2.0;
- the beneficiary does not meet the criteria in Section 3.0;
- the service duplicates another provider’s service; or
- the service is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial. ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 4.1, effective 12/15/2023)

## Governing coverage rule

The policy’s coverage rule is that emergency ambulance services are covered only to the extent necessary to **screen and stabilize** the beneficiary; no prior authorization is required if a prudent layperson would reasonably believe an emergency medical condition existed; and payment is based on retrospective review of the presenting history and symptoms. Services outside the covered criteria are not covered. ([Ambulance Services](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/15-ambulance-services/download?attachment), § 3.2, § 3.2.1, effective 12/15/2023)

I checked for amendments to Policy 15, and the current authoritative document is **Ambulance Services**, effective **12/15/2023**.

per_question.question: Are there quantity limits on prescription drugs under NC Medicaid, and when is prior authorization required for pharmacy claims?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. Under **NC Medicaid Clinical Coverage Policy 9**, pharmacy claims can be subject to **quantity limits**, and **prior authorization (PA)** is required for drugs or categories that NC Medicaid places on its pharmacy prior-approval list. The current document I checked is **Policy 9, effective July 15, 2024**, and I found no listed amendments changing that conclusion. [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

## Quantity limits

Policy 9 expressly refers to **“quantity limitations”** for drugs. In section **5.4.3, Quantity and Episodic Drugs**, NC Medicaid addresses:

- “the applicability of **quantity limitations** of episodic drugs,”
- “**prior authorization criteria and requirements**,” and
- steps to minimize dispensing fees for drugs prescribed in limited quantities. [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

The policy also contains **early-refill limits** for some non-controlled medications. In the approved clarification-code section:

- a **vacation supply** early refill is limited to **one 5-consecutive-day occurrence each 365-day period** for non-controlled medications;
- a **lost prescription** override is limited to **one occurrence on one date of service each 365-day period** for non-controlled medications. [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

So, at a minimum, NC Medicaid policy confirms:
1. there are **quantity-limit rules** for at least some drugs, especially episodic drugs; and  
2. there are separate **early refill/override limits** for certain situations.

## When prior authorization is required

Under Policy 9, PA is required for drugs in NC Medicaid’s **“Pharmacy Prior Approval Drugs and Criteria”** list. That list includes many specific drugs and classes, such as:

- GLP-1 receptor agonists and combinations
- hepatitis C medications
- growth hormones
- opioid analgesics
- opioid dependence therapy agents
- PCSK9 inhibitors
- triptans
- Synagis
- Botox/Myobloc/Dysport/Xeomin
- Epidiolex initial criteria
- cystic fibrosis drugs
- and many others. [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

Policy 9 also states in **5.0 / 5.1 Prior Authorization** that PA applies when there are:

- new variations of products already in the marketplace,
- new indications for products already in the marketplace,
- changes in indications for products, and
- changes in dosing for products already in the marketplace. [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

In addition, section **3.2.3** shows that NC Medicaid allows requests for **exceptions** to FDA/NC Medicaid drug criteria approval, but those requests must be supported by medical-necessity documentation, explanation of failed or inappropriate alternatives, and supporting compendia or peer-reviewed literature. [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

## Important distinction: quantity limits vs. PA

These are related but not identical:

- **Quantity limits** restrict how much of a drug can be dispensed or covered in a given circumstance.
- **Prior authorization** applies when the drug or claim falls into a category that Medicaid requires to be approved before payment.

A pharmacy claim can be denied or suspended for either reason. Policy 9’s request section indicates that if PA has not been obtained, the point-of-sale system may return messages such as **“PA REQ. PRESCRIBER CALL CSC”** or **“CLAIM DENIED. PA LIMITS EXCEEDED.”** [Lock-in Program](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/9-outpatient-pharmacy-program/download?attachment)

## Bottom line

- **Yes, NC Medicaid does impose quantity limits on some prescription drugs.**
- **Prior authorization is required when the drug or drug class appears in NC Medicaid’s pharmacy prior-approval criteria, and also in situations involving new products/indications/dosing changes described in Policy 9.**

2. the **rules for emergency 72-hour supplies when PA is pending or unavailable**.

per_question.question: Under what conditions can speech therapy be provided via telehealth under NC Medicaid?
per_question.agent_answer:
Speech therapy can be provided by telehealth under NC Medicaid when it is a covered speech/language evaluation or treatment service, is medically necessary, and the provider determines telehealth can be used safely and effectively for that beneficiary. NC Medicaid also imposes limits: telehealth is generally supposed to supplement, not replace, in-person care unless in-person care is unavailable or contraindicated. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (effective Feb. 1, 2025; current); [Clinical Coverage Policy 1-H](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment) (effective Feb. 1, 2025; current).

## Conditions NC Medicaid states for speech therapy via telehealth

Under **Clinical Coverage Policy 10A**, a “select set” of speech and language evaluation and treatment interventions may be delivered by telehealth, as described in **Clinical Coverage Policy 1-H**. Telehealth delivery **may be medically necessary** when:

- the beneficiary’s medical condition is such that **exposure to others should be avoided**, or
- the beneficiary’s location is **remote or underserved**, so access to appropriately qualified providers is limited.  
  [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (“Telehealth” subsection; effective Feb. 1, 2025; current).

Policy 10A says these criteria must be considered:

- **Unless in-person care is contraindicated or unavailable, telehealth must be an adjunct to in-person care, not a replacement.**
- **Telehealth must be in the beneficiary’s best interest, not for therapist convenience.**
- **Telehealth must never be used solely to increase therapist productivity.**  
  [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment) (“Telehealth” subsection; effective Feb. 1, 2025; current).

## Additional telehealth requirements from Policy 1-H

Because Policy 10A incorporates **Clinical Coverage Policy 1-H**, the provider also must satisfy the general telehealth criteria in that policy, including:

- the service must be able to be delivered **safely and effectively** by telehealth;
- the provider must consider the beneficiary’s **behavioral, physical, and cognitive abilities** to participate;
- the beneficiary’s **safety** must be considered in light of the service’s complexity;
- if a caregiver/facilitator is needed, the provider must consider that person’s **ability and safety**;
- the service must conform to **professional standards of care**, scope of practice, licensing rules, and other applicable federal/state/institutional requirements;
- the provider must **obtain and document verbal or written consent** (or document why consent could not be obtained in extenuating circumstances);
- the beneficiary is **not required** to use telehealth and must be allowed access to **in-person services if requested**;
- the provider must verify identity using **two points of identification** before starting the telehealth service; and
- the provider must protect **privacy and confidentiality** to the best of their ability.  
  [Clinical Coverage Policy 1-H](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment) § 3.2.1 (effective Feb. 1, 2025; current).

## Bottom line

NC Medicaid allows speech therapy by telehealth only for certain covered speech/language services and only when telehealth is medically necessary and appropriate for the beneficiary. As a rule, telehealth should supplement in-person care, not replace it, unless in-person care is unavailable or contraindicated. The provider must also meet the general telehealth safeguards in Policy 1-H. [Clinical Coverage Policy 10A](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/10a-outpatient-specialized-therapies/download?attachment); [Clinical Coverage Policy 1-H](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/1h-telehealth-virtual-communications-and-remote-patient-monitoring/download?attachment).

per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal Medicaid managed care law, there is **not an across-the-board mandatory minimum MLR that every state must impose**. What federal law does require is that the state ensure each Medicaid managed care organization calculates and reports an MLR. If a state **chooses** to require a minimum MLR in its contracts, that minimum must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8(a), (c).

## Federal rule

### What is always required
Federal law requires the state, through its contracts, to ensure that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR for each MLR reporting year. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8(a).

### What is conditional
Federal law says that **if a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR**, that minimum must be **equal to or higher than 85 percent**. The regulation ties that 85% figure to the actuarial soundness standard in § 438.4(b). [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8(c).

So the precise federal answer is:

- **MLR reporting/calculation:** required.
- **Minimum threshold:** only required if the state adopts one by contract.
- **If adopted, floor = 85%.** [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8(a), (c).

Federal oversight rules also require annual state reporting to CMS summarizing each plan’s MLR results, including the numerator, denominator, MLR percentage, member months, and any remittances owed. And if the state requires remittances for failure to meet the state’s minimum MLR, the state must reimburse CMS for the federal share and submit a separate methodology report. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.74(a)-(b).

## How North Carolina implements it

North Carolina’s implementation evidence here is in its CHIP managed care state plan amendment materials. In that document, NC states that:

- its rates are designed to reasonably achieve a medical loss ratio; and
- if an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP owes a remittance for not meeting the minimum MLR required by the state, NC will:
  - reimburse CMS for the federal share of the remittance, accounting for matching-rate differences; and
  - submit a separate report describing how the state and federal shares were determined, along with the annual report to CMS. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment), § 3.3.

That mirrors the federal oversight/remittance framework in § 438.74. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.74(b); [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment), § 3.3.

## Bottom line

- **Federal law does not itself impose a universal mandatory 85% minimum on every Medicaid managed care organization in every state.**
- Federal law **does require MLR calculation and reporting**.
- If a state imposes a minimum MLR, it must be **at least 85%**.
- North Carolina implements that framework by assuring rate development aimed at achieving MLR standards and by adopting the federal remittance/reporting approach when a plan fails to meet the state-required minimum. [42 CFR Part 438](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438), § 438.8(a), (c), § 438.74; [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment), § 3.3.

One caution: the NC document I could verify here is a **CHIP managed care SPA**, not a separate NC Medicaid contract provision for PHPs/MCOs. Based on the text retrieved, I can confirm NC has adopted the federal remittance/reporting framework in that managed care implementation document, but I could not verify from the retrieved text alone whether NC’s current Medicaid managed care contracts set a specific minimum MLR percentage beyond the federal floor rule.

per_question.question: What are the specific criteria for NC Medicaid coverage of CAR-T cell therapy?
per_question.agent_answer:
NC Medicaid covers CAR-T cell therapy when the beneficiary meets the policy’s general coverage rules and the CAR-T treatment meets the policy’s specific CAR-T criteria. The core CAR-T-specific criteria are:

- the CAR T-cell therapy must be **approved by the U.S. FDA**;
- it must be **administered according to the FDA-approved guidelines** for:
  - indications and usage,
  - dosage and administration,
  - dosage forms and strengths, and
  - warnings and precautions; and
- it must be **administered at a certified or authorized treatment center**. If the therapy is subject to an FDA-required **REMS** program, the treatment center must be enrolled in that REMS, and providers must be trained to manage **cytokine release syndrome (CRS)** and **neurological toxicities**.  
  ([CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), effective 2025-04-01, §§ 3.2, 3.2.1)

In addition, the policy’s general covered-service criteria apply. The service must be:

- individualized, specific, and consistent with the beneficiary’s symptoms or confirmed diagnosis;
- safely furnishable, with no equally effective and more conservative or less costly treatment available statewide; and
- furnished in a manner not primarily for the convenience of the beneficiary, caretaker, or provider.  
  ([CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), effective 2025-04-01, § 3.1)

## When CAR-T is not covered
The policy also identifies several situations where CAR-T is not covered, including when:

- the therapy is **not FDA approved**;
- it is being used **outside FDA guidelines** for indications/usage, dosage/administration, or dosage forms/strengths;
- a therapy that requires REMS is administered at a facility **not enrolled in that REMS**;
- the beneficiary is seeking **repeat treatment after having received another CAR-T therapy previously**;
- the beneficiary’s psychosocial history limits ability to comply with pre- and post-infusion care; or
- current beneficiary or caretaker non-compliance makes adherence to the treatment regimen improbable.  
  ([CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), effective 2025-04-01, § 4.2.1)

More generally, CAR-T is also not covered if the beneficiary does not meet Section 2.0 eligibility requirements, does not meet Section 3.0 criteria, if the service duplicates another provider’s service, or if it is experimental, investigational, or part of a clinical trial.  
([CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), effective 2025-04-01, § 4.1)

## Documentation typically required for approval
For prior approval, NC Medicaid requires documentation including:

- a physician-signed **letter of medical necessity** documenting past chemotherapy regimens and dates, clinical and social history, and indications for CAR-T;
- verification that the administering facility is a **qualified or authorized treatment center**;
- recent **HIV and hepatitis serologies**;
- diagnostic and procedure results, including **bone marrow biopsy** if applicable; and
- a complete **psychological and social evaluation**, including compliance history, support network, post-treatment care plan, and relevant mental health, substance use, or legal history.  
  ([CAR-T Cell Therapy](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/11a-17-car-t-cell-therapy/download?attachment), effective 2025-04-01, § 5.2.2)

per_question.question: Can an NC Innovations waiver participant request services that exceed their individual base budget, and what happens if they believe their needs cannot be met within the budget?
per_question.agent_answer:
Yes. An NC Innovations participant may request services that cost more than their individual base budget if they believe their needs cannot be met within that budget. The base budget is a guideline, not a hard cap. If the LME/MCO determines the requested services are medically necessary, the services must be authorized even if they exceed the base budget. If the request is denied, the individual must be told why and how to appeal, and the policy also provides for filing a grievance about the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## What the policy says

Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P states:

- the participant “may request services that cost in excess of his or her base budget if he or she believes his or her needs cannot be met within his or her base budget”;
- “the results of the SIS and the base budget are guidelines that do not constitute a binding limit on the amount of services that may be requested or authorized”; and
- if the LME/MCO finds the services medically necessary, “they will be authorized, regardless of the base budget.” Effective 2016-11-01; current per amendment check. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

The same policy also says that if any service authorization request is denied, the LME/MCO must notify the individual of:

- the reasons for the decision,
- how to appeal, and
- how to file a grievance regarding the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)

## If the person says their needs cannot be met within budget

Under federal HCBS waiver rules, services must be provided under a written person-centered service plan, and the planning process must offer informed choices and include a way for the individual to request updates to the plan as needed. [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

So, practically, the participant can:

- ask for a revised ISP/person-centered plan reflecting the unmet needs,
- request the medically necessary services even if they exceed the base budget,
- seek review through the LME/MCO if those needs are disputed, and
- appeal a denial or file a grievance regarding the base budget. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment) [42 CFR Part 441](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-441)

## Related detail in 8-P

Policy 8-P also recognizes that some requests may involve needs beyond the assigned Individual Budget Tool, including examples such as behavioral needs, medical needs, and approved post-secondary services requiring funding beyond the assigned budget tool. Effective 2016-11-01; current per amendment check. [Clinical Coverage Policy 8-P, North Carolina Innovations](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/8-p-north-carolina-innovations/download?attachment)
